Reading the CTC piece by Cerwyn Moore: "The Threat From Swarm Attacks" Questions that arise: Are swarm attacks and fidayin attacks conceptually the same? Are there junctures and disjunctures? Would the use of the term "swarm attacks" be better suited to a paper that aspires to a more comprehensive survey/analysis of these types of attacks?

(Wikipedia article on swarming as a military tactic: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swarming_%28military%29 )

**Shared characteristics between swarm and fidayin notions: **

  • Tactical implementation
  • Deliberate asymmetry or operationally internalized asymmetry
  • Fluidity in terms of tactics, operational space, targeting, weapons and equipment

Differences for swarming:

  • Generic nomenclature (which is what makes this term desirable for a project with broad aims)
  • Limited immediate strategic implication (regardless of the outcome of a swarming operation in a conventional military situation, it may or may not have dramatic effects on the strategic scale)
  • Limits on "acceptable" losses (classic military doctrine requires commanders to prevent personnel and resources being disproportionately expended vis-a-vis the strategic importance of a target or operational objective)
  • Asymmetry works for both outnumbered and superior forces (A superior force can use swarming with facility/efficacy, so can an inferior force... Depending on the combat realities but based on the fact that open warfare is being conducted)
  • Applicable to a classic battlespace as well as other types
  • Ambiguous to no direct impact on public response/"return to normal" (Since swarm attacks are classically part of open warfare, it is not supposed that the public is a target audience so much as it maybe a component of the adversary's military efforts... In other words, attacks are expected and their variable nature may have a limited psychological and social impact)
  • Hard targets (expectation of defensive efforts)

Differences for fidayin:

  • Direct (or indirect) strategic impact possible and scalable (PNS Mehran and Mumbai both suggest attempts to immediately alter the strategic situation in jihadists' favor; the attack on Pak GHQ and elements of the PNS Mehran attack suggest the ambition to force release of important sub-strategic jihadist actors)
  • Immediate ideological implications (the root verb of "fidayi" means to dare one's life, deeper intentionality is suggested)
  • Specific nomenclature (Fidayin equates to Islamic context)
  • Fidayin are "told to survive," but in practice and due to ideological underpinnings and semantics, prone to heavy or complete losses as acceptable -- demonstration of "invincibility, intentionality"
  • Asymmetric for the outnumbered, but not as well-wielded in a conventional military context (element of surprise and backdrop of relative security stability is a necessary characteristic)
  • Direct, geometric effect on public response (long term security instability through multiple vectors, greater media sensationalizing possible, confusion of security forces/jurisdictional roles in peace time situation, "return to normal" prolonged extensively)
  • Soft targets (expectation of lesser defensive efforts, passive security)

Before considering cooking it, you need a grinder capable to transform seed in flour.

I personally use a Thermomix.

You will need:

  • 200g almonds
  • 150g pumpkin seeds

Grind this until it's pulverized into flour.

Then add the following in the blender:

  • ~10g yeast diluted in 5cl warm water
  • 2 eggs
  • 5 to 10g salt
  • 65g cottage cheese

Mix this (your blender doesn't need to be on full speed for this) until it's homogenous.

This will be sticky so use a silicon mold and take your time pouring it from the blender.

Oven -> 150°C for around 45 minutes.

Oddly enough the yeast elevate the crust.

You'll notice this bread is green but it's actually very tasty.
